newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA's Macfarlane says wage rises a problem.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA's Macfarlane says wage rises a problem.

text.p: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Ian Macfarlane said on Thursday wage bargaining tensions were clouding the outlook for inflation and unemployment.
Macfarlane said excessive wage increases in sectors of the Australian economy which remain relatively closed could lead to higher inflation, making monetary policy management difficult.

In a speech to the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia (CEDA), he said average wages had not grown at too fast a pace and this had allowed the central bank to cut rates in July and November this year.
The official cash rate now stands at 6.5 percent, having been cut by 50 basis points each time this calendar year.

"The tensions in the wage enterprise bargaining area remain, however, and cloud the outlook for inflation, but more particularly for unemployment," said Macfarlane, who added he was disappointed Australia's unemployment rate of 8.8 percent had not fallen further.
Excessive wage rises in those industry sectors open to international and domestic competition were more of a concern because of their potential impact on unemployment rather than inflation, he said.
"In other sectors where the economy is still relatively closed, excessive wage increases will be potentially inflationary," he said.
"This makes it difficult for monetary policy," he said.

"We do not know the extent to which excessively high wage settlements will spread to other parts of the economy, particularly if executive pay sets a bad example, as seems to be the case at present," he added.

Macfarlane said adjustment to the low inflation environment in Australia had not been uniform, citing in particular wage bargaining and the understandable transitional problems associated with a move from centralised wage fixing to enterprise, or workplace, bargaining.

He said the central bank's monetary policy was conducted on the basis that inflation would average 2.5 percent annually over the medium term. "Some people have interpreted an inflation target to mean that monetary policy is only worried about inflation, and that it is therefore anti-growth," he said.
"We do not seek to keep within a narrow target band on a period-by-period basis," Macfarlane said.
"It (the target) also recognises that, in the event of a large shock, it is sensible to bring inflation back on track over time, rather than by some 'cold turkey' measures."
